extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; scholars and anyone studying theories of sovereignty and commonwealth
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and principles for instituting and exercising sovereign power in a commonwealth (Hobbesian theory). Covers generation, definition, rights and limits of the sovereign, indivisibility, succession, and comparisons of forms of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons humans require a sovereign (contrast with irrational creatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst creatures other than man, the common good coincides with private good; they lack reason to dispute administration; they lack the art of words to misrepresent Good and Evil; they cannot distinguish between injury and damage; their agreement is natural. Man, however, compares himself with others, relishes eminence, sees faults in administration, uses language to discontent men, distinguishes injury from damage, and his agreements are artificial (by Covenant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contrasts are offered as the ground why men need, beyond mere covenant, a Common Power to keep them in awe and direct actions to the common benefit; they justify instituting a sovereign to prevent discord, faction, and civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Generation Of A Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to erect such a Common Power is to confer all their power and strength upon one man, or upon one Assembly of men, that may reduce all their Wills, by plurality of voices, unto one Will: to appoint one man, or Assembly of men, to beare their Person; and every one to owne, and acknowledge himselfe to be Author of whatsoever he that so beareth their Person, shall Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation requires each person to 'authorise and give up my Right of Governing myself, to this Man, or to this Assembly' so that the multitude united in one Person becomes a COMMON-WEALTH (CIVITAS). The passage provides the precise covenantal language and mechanism (mutual authorization) by which the sovereign is instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition Of A Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A Common-wealth is 'One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author, to the end he may use the strength and means of them all, as he shall think expedient, for their Peace and Common Defence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal definition: the commonwealth's essence resides in one representative Person authorized by all; the sovereign's acts are the acts of the body politic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soveraigne and Subject; two ways to attain sovereign power
rubrics_metrics.description: He that carryeth this Person is called SOVERAIGNE; attainment is by (1) Naturall force (acquisition by conquest or subjection), or (2) by Institution (men agree voluntarily to submit to some Man or Assembly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes commonwealth by Acquisition (subjugation) and commonwealth by Institution (covenantal consent); the subsequent chapter focuses on commonwealth by Institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects Cannot Change The Forme Of Government
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Institution of a Common-wealth are derived all the Rights, and Facultyes of him on whom the Soveraigne Power is conferred; those that have already Instituted a Common-wealth cannot lawfully make a new Covenant to be obedient to any other without his permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subjects have covenanted to own sovereign actions, to depose or transfer sovereignty without permission is injustice; attempting to depose the sovereign would be to take away what was granted and is thus unjust, and would revert disputes to force (the Sword).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soveraigne Power Cannot Be Forfeited
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Right of bearing the Person of them all is given by Covenant of one to another (not of him to them), there can happen no breach of Covenant on the part of the Soveraigne; consequently no subject can, by pretence of forfeiture, be freed from subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: sovereign makes no prior covenant with subjects; covenants are words backed only by public force. If subjects claimed forfeiture, no judge could decide without returning to force; thus forfeiture as a legal means of removal is impossible under this account.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Man Can Without Injustice Protest Against The Institution Declared By The Major Part
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the major part hath by consenting voices declared a Soveraigne; he that dissented must now consent with the rest and be contented to avow all the actions he shall do, or else justly be destroyed by the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacit consent of attending a congregation implies consenting to the majoritarian decree; refusal to stand by the decree is contrary to covenant and therefore unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Soveraign's Actions Cannot Be Justly Accused By The Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Subject is by institution Author of all the Actions, and Judgements of the Soveraigne; it followes that whatsoever he doth, it can be no injury to any of his Subjects; he that complaineth of injury from his Soveraigne, complaineth of that whereof he himselfe is Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'iniquity' (moral badness) from 'injury' (wrong); sovereign may commit iniquity but not injustice in the proper signification, since his acts are those of the subjects themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatsoever The Soveraign Doth, Is Unpunishable By The Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: No man that hath Soveraigne power can justly be put to death, or otherwise in any manner by his Subjects punished, for to punish another is to punish oneself because each Subject is author of sovereign actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of authorship: subjects cannot lawfully punish the sovereign for sovereign acts; such punishment would be self-punishment and so unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Soveraign Is Judge Of What Is Necessary For The Peace And Defence Of His Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongeth of Right to whatsoever Man, or Assembly that hath the Soveraignty, to be Judge both of the meanes of Peace and Defence; and also of the hindrances, and disturbances of the same; and to do whatsoever he shall think necessary to be done, both beforehand . . . and for the recovery of the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the end (peace and defence) is the sovereign's, he has right to the means; this grants broad discretionary authority to act preventively or recoveringly for public security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soveraigne as Censor: Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught
rubrics_metrics.description: It is annexed to the Soveraignty, to be Judge of what Opinions and Doctrines are averse, and what conducing to Peace; and consequently, on what occasions, how farre, and what, men are to be trusted withall, in speaking to Multitudes of people; and who shall examine the Doctrines of all bookes before they be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign authority over doctrine is justified by the link between opinions and actions; false or peace-repugnant doctrines may be regulated for the sake of public peace. The text permits suppression or regulation of doctrines to prevent discord and civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of making Rules of Propriety (what is mine and thine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annexed to the Soveraigntie, the whole power of prescribing the Rules, whereby every man may know, what Goods he may enjoy and what Actions he may doe, without being molested by any of his fellow Subjects: This Proprietie (or Meum and Tuum) ... are the Civill Lawes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign prescribes the civil rules that define property, lawful and unlawful actions; property and civil law are instruments of peace and depend on sovereign power to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of All Judicature And Decision Of Controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Annexed to the Soveraigntie, the Right of Judicature; that is to say, of hearing and deciding all Controversies, concerning Law, either Civill, or naturall, or concerning Fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a single authority to decide controversies, protection against injury is impossible and the rule of law cannot function; judicature is essential to prevent return to private force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Making War, And Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Annexed to the Soveraignty, the Right of making Warre, and Peace with other Nations, and Common-wealths; to judge when it is for the publique good, and how great forces are to be assembled, armed, and payd for that end; and to levy mony upon the Subjects, to defray the expenses thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign controls foreign policy and military command, including taxation to fund defence; command of the militia or arms equates to sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Choosing All Counsellours, And Ministers, Both Of Peace, And Warre
rubrics_metrics.description: Annexed to the Soveraignty, the choosing of all Councellours, Ministers, Magistrates, and Officers, both in peace, and Warre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign discretion to select advisors and officials is part of his charge to effect the common peace and defence; staffing choices are essential means to ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Rewarding, And Punishing, Arbitrarily Where No Former Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Committed to the Soveraign the Power of Rewarding with riches, or honour; and of Punishing with corporall, or pecuniary punishment, or with ignominy every Subject according to the Lawe he hath formerly made; or if there be no Law made, according as he shall judge most to conduce to the encouraging of men to serve the Common-wealth, or deterring of them from doing dis-service to the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign may apply punitive or reward measures within the bounds of laws he has made; where no prior law exists he may act arbitrarily as he judges fit for public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Honour And Order (titles, public rank, and enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongeth also to the Soveraign to give titles of Honour; and to appoint what Order of place, and dignity, each man shall hold; and what signes of respect, in publique or private meetings, they shall give to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign establishes public hierarchy and honors to manage emulation, factions, and preserve order—these laws of honour require force to execute.

rubrics_metrics.name: These Rights Are Indivisible
rubrics_metrics.description: These are the Rights which make the Essence of Soveraignty; and which are the markes, whereby a man may discern in what Man, or Assembly the Soveraign Power is placed. For these are incommunicable, and inseparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed sovereign rights are essential and cannot be separated without undermining the sovereign's ability to preserve peace; partition of rights leads to ineffectiveness and potential civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Grants Void Without Direct Renouncing Of Sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Because they are essential and inseparable Rights, if any of them seem to be granted away, yet if the Soveraigne Power itself be not in direct termes renounced, and the name of Soveraigne no more given by the Grantees to him that Grants them, the Grant is voyd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial grants of sovereign prerogatives are ineffective unless sovereignty itself is directly renounced; transferring particular privileges does not transfer the sovereign office absent explicit renunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Power And Honour Of Subjects Vanisheth In The Presence Of The Soveraigne
rubrics_metrics.description: This great Authority being indivisible, there is little ground for the opinion that Sovereign Kings are less powerful than all their subjects together; the power of all together is the sovereign's power, and the honour of the sovereign ought to be greater than that of any or all the subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign is fountain of honour; dignities are his creatures; in his presence subjects' power and honour are null—this is normative instruction about the social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Power Less Harmful Than Its Absence (argument for coercion/taxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though subjects may be obnoxious to the lusts of sovereigns, the worst that can happen under sovereign rule is less than the miseries of civil war and absence of government; apparent grievances (taxes) are small compared to the calamities avoided by a coercive sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evaluates trade-offs: sovereign levies and demands are justified as necessary burdens to avoid the far greater evils of war and lawlessness; appeals to moral/civil science to see long-term benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Different Formes Of Common-wealth: Three kinds only
rubrics_metrics.description: The Representative must be One man, or More: if More, either All or a Part. When the Representative is One man, the Common-wealth is a MONARCHY; when an Assembly of All that will come together, a DEMOCRACY; when an Assembly of a Part only, an ARISTOCRACY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomy of government forms: three exhaustive types are defined by who bears the person of the commonwealth (one, some, or all).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny and Oligarchy are names of disliked forms, not distinct kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny and Oligarchy are not names of other Formes of Government, but of the same Formes misliked: those discontented under Monarchy call it Tyranny, those displeased with Aristocracy call it Oligarchy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminological guidance: critical epithets reflect opinion, not different constitutional kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate Representatives are Dangerous (no two sovereigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is already erected a Soveraign Power, there can be no other Representative of the same people, except to certain ends limited by the sovereign; erecting two sovereigns would divide indivisible power and reduce the multitude to war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against multiple general representations; local deputies or ministers exist but cannot become another general sovereign; the presence of more than one sovereign power risks civil conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Criteria: Monarchy vs Sovereign Assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the three kinds is of convenience and aptitude to produce Peace and Security. Points: (1) In Monarchy private and public interest often align (monarch's welfare tied to subjects'); (2) Monarch can take counsel when, whom, and where he pleases, with secrecy and expertise; (3) Monarch's resolutions subject only to human inconstancy vs assemblies' additional inconstancy from number; (4) Monarch cannot disagree with himself as an assembly can; (5) Monarch may abuse power to favor friends but assemblies can be equally or more corrupt/unstable; (6) Risk of infant succession exists in monarchy but assemblies also may require temporary dictators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides evaluative criteria for choosing a form: unity of interests, quality and secrecy of counsel, stability of decisions, risk profiles (favouritism, infant succession), and practical efficacy in large commonwealths. It also notes elective or limited monarchies and how succession rules affect sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective and Limited Monarchies are to be understood as variations of monarchy or ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective Kings, where kings have sovereign power for a time, are not sovereigns if they cannot appoint successors; if he can appoint successor he is hereditary; if not, someone else must have the right to give sovereignty after his death or the commonwealth dies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies how elective or time-limited offices relate to the locus of sovereignty: without power to secure succession, the elected's position is that of a minister, not sovereign; failure to provide succession risks collapse into war.
